title: Insurers warn of battery fire crisis
full_text:
Australia’s biggest insurers say a regulatory lag has sparked a national crisis as claims from explosive lithium-ion battery-linked fires almost doubled in the past three years.
The Insurance Council of Australia says some insurers are increasing their premiums to reflect the risk they take on, as fire-damage claims become more expensive thanks to the battery boom.
Market heavyweights Suncorp, IAG and Mitti say that a flood of cheap lithium-powered products ranging from power tools and e-scooters to replacement chargers is a threat to buildings that were never designed to contain volatile thermal runaway fires. They believe the problem will intensify due to the Black Friday sales, held later this month, when people seek bargains online.
China is the world’s biggest developer and manufacturer of lithium battery technology.
Insurers say aftermarket chargers and overcharging can lead to thermal runaway within lithium-ion batteries, causing a fire to reignite – even when they appear to be extinguished. Many airlines now ban the use of power banks on flights, citing their fire risk.
The federal government has been encouraging Australians to electrify their homes to mitigate soaring power bills. Demand for its Cheaper Home Batteries scheme – launched in July last year – was higher than forecast, and its initial $2.3bn budget was tripled.
Suncorp executive general manager of home insurance Anna Cartwright said home insurance claims linked to lithium-ion battery fires almost doubled between 2023 and 2026. Cheap e-bikes, e-scooters and power tools were among the top culprits.
“The damage these fires cause is becoming more severe,” Ms Cartwright said. “Most lithium-ion batteries are safe when used correctly, but the consequences can be devastating when a battery is damaged, paired with the wrong charger, or charged or stored unsafely. These fires can spread incredibly quickly and can even reignite after they appear to be out.” Ms Cartwright urged buyers not to purchase cheap products.
“As Australians shop the Black Friday and Christmas sales, price shouldn’t be the only consideration,” she said. “Buy from reputable brands and retailers, check for appropriate safety certifications and always follow the manufacturer’s guidance on charging, use and storage.” IAG, Australia’s biggest insurer, said “Australia’s lithium-ion battery market is growing faster than safety standards and consumer education”.
It’s not just a problem in homes. Mitti – formerly Safety Culture, which has a multibillion-dollar global workplace insurer – said many commercial buildings were not designed to be battery powered. “Lithium-ion batteries are in almost every commercial workplace now, from retail stock and e-bikes to forklifts and power tools, so the question isn’t whether a business has them, it’s how they’re stored, charged and looked after,” said Mitti Insurance managing director Australia Dan Cummins.
“One thing that often gets missed is the building itself. Most businesses think about the equipment, but a lot of Australian commercial premises were never designed for this technology.
“We’re adding lithium to older electrical, ventilation and fire-protection systems that weren’t built with it in mind, and that can compound the risk.” Mitti now asks potential clients questions about lithium-ion batteries when writing commercial insurance policies and provides “quick 15-minute assessments” to help spot “hidden dangers”.
“When we look at a business, we want to know where batteries are charged and kept, how damaged or returned units are isolated, whether staff know what to do, and whether inspections are written down and followed up,” Mr Cummins said.
“The businesses that can show us those habits day to day are in a much better position to prevent an incident, and to have an informed conversation with their insurer.
“Insurers should be helping policyholders find and fix these risks long before a claim is made.” An Insurance Council of Australia spokeswoman said failure to disclose battery-powered items might lead to claims not being covered.
“Each insurer sets its own premiums based on risk, and this growing risk may be reflected in pricing,” the spokeswoman said. “As with any addition to your home and contents, we encourage people to tell their insurer if they own an e-bike or e-scooter. Devices that have been modified after purchase, or don’t meet the legal definition of an e-bike, may not be covered.”
